name: Challenges in Pakistani Mid-Tier Private Schools

content.title: Challenges in Pakistani Mid-Tier Private Schools
content.summary: Dr Saulat Pervez shares insights on private schooling at AKU-IED's Kazim Bacchus Research Seminar

media.alt: Challenges in Pakistani Mid-Tier Private Schools

content.text: AKU-IED's recent Kazim Bacchus Research Seminar featured a thought-provoking presentation by Dr Saulat Pervez, a researcher from the International Institute of Islamic Thought (IIIT) in Virginia, USA. The seminar, titled 'Locating Pakistani Mid-Tier Private Schools in Local & Global Educational Discourses,' provided an in-depth analysis based on Dr Pervez's extensive research and experiences in Pakistan and other parts of the world.

Dr Pervez, with her vast experience in Karachi's private schooling sector, explored the complexities of postcolonial cultures influencing social class, language disparities, and reading attitudes. She delved into the challenges posed by the dominance of English, which marginalizes the native language, Urdu, and hampers the development of reading and writing cultures in both languages. Her research is particularly focused on bi/multilingual contexts and how these dynamics affect educational outcomes.

The hybrid session allowed both in-person and virtual attendees to engage actively. She critically examined the prevalent classification of English-medium private schools in Pakistan, challenging the simplistic elite/non-elite and rich/poor dichotomies. She highlighted the existence of middle-tier English-medium private schools that do not fit neatly into these binary categories.

Dr Pervez provided a nuanced view of these middle-tier schools, noting that the families of students in these institutions primarily speak Urdu or regional languages at home, with parents typically holding tertiary degrees and middle management positions. This contrasts with parents of low-fee school students, who often lack education and work in manual labor roles.

Her presentation also placed middle-tier schools within the global educational discourse on language immersion and submersion, exploring whether the language learning experiences of Pakistani students in these schools are additive or subtractive. Drawing from her personal experiences as an educator and parent, as well as empirical findings from a case study at a middle-tier school in Karachi, Dr Pervez emphasized the need to move beyond simplistic binaries. She advocated for a deeper exploration of how bilingualism/multilingualism impacts a wide range of Pakistani students, not just those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds.

The seminar concluded with a lively Q&A session, reflecting the audience's keen interest in the topic. The presentation provided valuable insights into middle-tier schools, urging educators and researchers to adopt a more nuanced approach in understanding and addressing the educational needs of Pakistani students.
